CONNECTION NOTE (under 200 characters, no link)
Saw your post on the PF audit headaches at your Nashik plant. I build PF compliance software in Pune and fight the same fires most weeks. Would be glad to connect.

MESSAGE 1 (after she accepts)
Thanks for connecting, [first name].

Your post reminded me which checks usually decide how long a PF inspection drags on. I've put them on one page (attached):
- ECR headcount against payroll
- a UAN for every contract worker
- allowances that count as PF wages
- challan dates against the 15th

It's yours to use, no follow-up call needed.

Is most of the pain coming from contract workers or from your own rolls?

MESSAGE 2 (no reply, four working days later)
One more thing that helps plants your size. [Customer example: 350-worker forging unit in Chakan] now matches each contractor's monthly ECR against its own gate-entry count before clearing the contractor's bill. [Result: their last inspection closed in one visit.]

MESSAGE 3 (optional, a week later)
I'll stop here so I don't clutter your inbox. If PF audits now sit with someone else on your team, tell me who and I'll send them the checklist instead.

samples.brief: Model Common App personal essay (prompt: a challenge or setback and what you learned) for a fictional 17-year-old from Jamshedpur applying to US engineering programmes; the story is rebuilding the order book of her mother's tailoring shop on WhatsApp after a fire. English (US spelling), 550-620 words, used as a teaching example in an admissions-coaching course, not for submission.
samples.text:
The order book survived the fire in the worst possible way. Its cover was fine. Its pages had fused into a brown brick that cracked when I tried to open it, and inside it were eleven years of my mother's work: blouse lengths, kurta chests, and the note she kept for Mrs. Hembram that said "left shoulder lower, don't mention it." I stood in the wet ash of Ma's shop in Sakchi, holding the brick, and realized that her customers were now names nobody had written down anywhere else.

The fire started in a meter board two shops down, in March of my junior year. Nobody was hurt. The two sewing machines could be repaired and the cloth could be reordered. What couldn't be replaced was the book, and the phone numbers were in it too. Wedding season starts in April, and wedding blouses are where Ma's year is made. Half-finished orders hung in plastic bags, and she had no way to reach the women who owned them. That evening she sat on the shop's step and said quietly that maybe it was time to stop.

My first plan was an engineer's plan, or what I thought one was. I'd build a database. I spent two nights on a spreadsheet with columns for neck depth and dart placement, then showed it to Ma. She looked at it the way she looks at a badly cut sleeve. "Who will fill this?" she asked. Not her. Not her customers, most of whom have never opened a spreadsheet.

That stung, because she was right. I had designed for the problem I found interesting, not for the person who had it. So I started again from what Ma already used every day: WhatsApp. Her customers were all on it. They already sent her photos of blouses they wanted copied. I set up a business account for the shop. For a week, Ma and I sat with the phone and the brick and pieced together what we could: a surname from a corner of a page, numbers from her call log, numbers from neighbors who knew someone's sister. I wrote one message in Hindi, short enough to read in a rickshaw: there was a fire, your order is safe, send your measurements or come in and we'll take them again for free.

Then I learned what the spreadsheet couldn't have taught me. People didn't answer the message. They answered Ma. They sent voice notes, long ones, about weddings and daughters-in-law and, somewhere in the middle, a waist size. So I stopped trying to make them fill anything. Every night I listened to the day's voice notes, typed each customer's measurements into a pinned note in her chat, and gave her a label. Ma did the talking. I did the typing.

By the peak of wedding season, most of her regulars were back. The new order book lives in two places now, on the phone and in a notebook, because Ma trusts paper and I've stopped arguing. She searches the labels herself and sends the "your blouse is ready" message without calling me in. Last month my cousin, who runs a sweet shop in Bistupur, asked me to set up the same system for his Diwali orders. The first thing I asked him wasn't which app he wanted. It was who would be typing.

I still have the brick. It sits on my desk beside my physics notes. When I sketch anything now, a circuit, a form, an app, I ask Ma's question before I ask mine: who will fill this? I want to study engineering because I love building things. I want to build them for the person holding the phone.

samples.brief: Four-page Instagram carousel comic (one page per 4:5 slide, 3-4 panels each) for a fictional Lucknow small-savings app, 'GullakPe': a chai-stall owner learns to set aside Rs 20 a day through UPI round-ups. Script format with PAGE / PANEL headings, panel descriptions in English, dialogue in Hinglish (Roman), final slide caption with the CTA.
samples.text:
MUNNA KI GULLAK
A GullakPe brand comic. Episode 1 of 1. 4 pages.
Format: Instagram carousel, one page per slide, 4:5 (1080 x 1350 px). Max 4 panels per slide, lettering large enough to read on a phone.
Art and tone: warm flat colour, monsoon-wet Lucknow street, expressive faces, gentle humour. Dialogue in Hinglish (Roman); keep spellings exactly as written.
Cast: MUNNA (40s, chai-stall owner, half-sleeve sweater over kurta, gamchha on shoulder). ZOYA (19, college student, regular customer, backpack, scooter helmet on her arm). KALLU (50s, paan-wala next door, always chewing).

PAGE 1 (3 panels)

Panel 1. WIDE. Early morning, a narrow lane in Aminabad, Lucknow. Rain drips off the tin roof of MUNNA's chai stall: wooden counter, aluminium kettle on a single-burner gas stove, a row of small glasses, a UPI QR stand taped to the counter. Behind him, on a shelf, a red clay gullak. MUNNA pours chai from a height into two glasses for two office-goers holding umbrellas.
1 CAPTION: Aminabad, Lucknow. Subah 7 baje.
2 OFFICE-GOER: Munna bhai, do kadak. UPI se.
3 SFX (phone): TING!

Panel 2. MEDIUM. The burner flame shrinks to a blue flicker and dies. MUNNA freezes mid-pour, kettle in hand, staring down at it.
4 SFX: phut... phut...
5 MUNNA: Arre nahi nahi. Aaj nahi.

Panel 3. CLOSE. MUNNA holds the clay gullak upside down and shakes it. A single ten-rupee coin drops onto the counter. His face: the embarrassment of a man who knew this already.
6 MUNNA (thought): Naya burner chhe sau ka. Aur gullak mein... das rupaye.
7 CAPTION: Roz kamaata tha. Bachta kuch nahi tha.

PAGE 2 (4 panels)

Panel 1. MEDIUM. KALLU's paan stall next door. KALLU counts six hundred-rupee notes into MUNNA's palm, smirking, cheek full of paan.
1 KALLU: Le lo. Mahine ke end tak lauta dena... byaaj ke saath.
2 MUNNA: Haan haan. Hamesha ki tarah.

Panel 2. MEDIUM. Back at the stall, a new burner burns bright. ZOYA scans the QR with one hand, holding her glass of chai in the other, and turns her phone towards MUNNA.
3 ZOYA: Bhaiya, aap bhi GullakPe laga lo. Mera roz ka chutta wahin jaata hai.
4 MUNNA: UPI mein chutta kahan hota hai, beta?

Panel 3. CLOSE. ZOYA's phone screen fills the panel. Draw the app clearly: a small red clay-gullak icon and one notification card.
5 PHONE SCREEN: ₹46 ka payment, ₹50 round-up. ₹4 aapki gullak mein.
6 ZOYA (off-panel): Har payment upar round hota hai. Jo bacha, gullak mein.

Panel 4. MEDIUM. MUNNA squints at his own phone; ZOYA leans over the counter to help. His thumb hovers over a slider on screen labelled "Roz ki limit: ₹20".
7 MUNNA: Sirf bees rupaye roz? Itne se kya hoga?
8 ZOYA: Ek mahina dekh lo, bhaiya.

PAGE 3 (3 panels)

Panel 1. MEDIUM. Morning. The milkman on his cycle, two steel cans hanging off the carrier. MUNNA scans the milkman's QR from behind his counter. His phone, propped on the counter, lights up.
1 CAPTION: Din 3.
2 PHONE SCREEN: ₹6 gullak mein.

Panel 2. MEDIUM. Evening, rain outside. MUNNA at a kirana counter with a sugar sack on his shoulder, paying by QR. He glances at his phone and smiles to himself.
3 CAPTION: Din 17.
4 PHONE SCREEN: Aaj ka ₹20 poora.
5 MUNNA (to himself): Pata bhi nahi chala.

Panel 3. CLOSE. Morning, the stall. The old aluminium kettle has split along the base; chai drips onto the counter in a brown line. MUNNA holds the kettle up, eyes wide, while KALLU leans into frame from the next stall, already reaching for his wallet.
6 CAPTION: Din 30.
7 SFX: tip... tip... tip...
8 KALLU: Phir se udhaar, Munna?

PAGE 4 (3 panels)

Panel 1. CLOSE. MUNNA's phone, GullakPe open. The clay-gullak icon is drawn full to the brim. MUNNA's thumb in the corner of the frame.
1 PHONE SCREEN: Aapki gullak: ₹600. 30 din, ₹20 roz.
2 MUNNA (off-panel): Chhe sau?

Panel 2. MEDIUM. A utensil shop in Aminabad. MUNNA pays by QR for a shiny new steel kettle. KALLU stands behind him, paan halfway to his mouth, eyebrows up.
3 KALLU: Is baar udhaar nahi chahiye?
4 MUNNA: Nahi Kallu bhai. Is baar apni gullak hai.

Panel 3. WIDE. Next morning. The stall is busy, the new kettle steaming on the burner, MUNNA pouring chai with a grin. The old clay gullak is back on the shelf with a small GullakPe sticker on it. ZOYA raises her glass to him.
5 ZOYA: Toh bhaiya, ek mahina ho gaya?
6 MUNNA: Agla mahina bhi. Ab bees nahi, tees.
7 CAPTION (CTA bar across the bottom of the slide): Aapka chutta bhi gullak ban sakta hai. GullakPe download karein, aaj se roz ₹20 bachayein. Link bio mein.

POST CAPTION
Munna bhai ki gullak mein das rupaye the. Tees din baad? Slide karke dekhiye.
Har UPI payment ka chutta, din ka ₹20, seedha aapki GullakPe gullak mein. App download karne ka link bio mein hai.

Chhapa Ghar, Instagram comment replies (5 drafts). Each reply under 50 words; reply language matches the comment.

1. Angry comment, delivery delay (English)
COMMENT: 9 days and still no kurta. Worst experience, never ordering again.
REPLY: Nine days is too long to wait for a kurta you've already paid for, and that's on us, not you. We've just sent you a DM. Share your order number there and we'll tell you today exactly where your parcel is.
Public close-out, posted after the DM fix: Update for anyone reading: sorted over DM and the kurta is on its way. Thank you for calling it out here.

2. Sizing question (Hinglish)
COMMENT: Meri height 5'2'' hai, ye kurta kitna lamba aayega? S lu ya M?
REPLY: Ye kurta [44 inch] lamba hai, toh 5'2'' par ghutne se thoda neeche tak aayega. Size height se nahi, bust se chuniye: [36 inch tak S, 38 tak M]. Apna bust naap DM kar dijiye, hum size confirm kar denge.

3. Compliment on the new print (English)
COMMENT: The new indigo dabu print is so pretty
REPLY: Thank you! Dabu is printed with a mud resist, so every piece cracks a little differently. Which colour should we try it in next?

4. Troll: 'overpriced' (Hinglish)
COMMENT: Itna mehenga? Sarojini mein 300 ka milta hai lol
REPLY: Sarojini ka 300 wala bhi apni jagah sahi hai. Hamare kurte mein har rang ka alag haath ka block lagta hai, aur agla rang tabhi chhapta hai jab pehla sookh jaaye. Isi mehnat ka daam hai. Chhapai ki reel dekhni ho toh bataiye?

5. Founder's outbound comment on a creator's slow-fashion post (English)
COMMENT: (Creator's post: why slow fashion means waiting longer for your clothes)
REPLY: From a block-print workshop in Jaipur: the slowest part isn't the printing, it's the drying. Each colour has to dry before the next block goes down. Would your followers wait a week for a kurta if they knew that's why?

samples.brief: Blog comparison 'Zoho Books vs Tally Prime for a 10-person Indian services firm (2026)' for the website of a Jaipur CA firm that advises small agencies. samples.text:
Zoho Books vs Tally Prime for a 10-person Indian services firm (2026)

Choosing accounting software for a ten-person agency or consultancy comes down to who needs access, how you bill clients, and how much you want the books tied to one PC.

Quick verdict

Pick Zoho Books if your team bills clients every month, works from more than one place, or wants partners and your CA to log in without waiting for a data file. Pick Tally Prime if one trained accountant does all the entry in one office and you want a licence you own and your auditor already knows. Neither wins everything. Tally is faster for a trained keyboard user. Zoho is easier to share.

Last checked: [DATE]. Prices and features below were read from the vendors' own pages on that date.

Disclosure: we are a Jaipur CA firm and our fee comes from our software-setup consultation. [Confirm before publishing: no reseller, referral or affiliate arrangement with Zoho or Tally Solutions.]

At a glance

| Criterion | Zoho Books | Tally Prime | Better for a 10-person services firm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | Browser and mobile apps | Windows desktop install | Zoho for remote teams, Tally for one office |
| How you pay | Monthly or annual plan [price as of DATE] | One-time licence plus optional support [price as of DATE] | Tally over 3+ years, Zoho if cash is tight |
| GST invoices, e-invoice, returns | Built in [plan needed: as of DATE] | Built in; some online steps use the vendor's connected services [as of DATE] | Tie |
| Recurring client invoices | Built in | [native option in current release: as of DATE] | Zoho |
| Payment links on invoices | Online gateways can be connected | [confirm: as of DATE] | Zoho |
| Multiple users | Role-based logins from anywhere | Multi-user licence on an office network | Zoho for remote, Tally inside one office |
| Entry speed, trained accountant | Form driven, shortcuts available | Keyboard-first vouchers | Tally |
| Auditor familiarity | Growing | Very high | Tally |
| Updates | Automatic | Manual install, new releases tied to the support plan | Zoho |

How we compared

Two of our accountants set up the same test firm in both products on [test date]. It had ten staff, six retainer clients billed monthly and two project clients billed by milestone. It also had four vendors with TDS on professional fees and one GST registration in Rajasthan. We used [Zoho Books plan] and [Tally Prime edition and release]. Every measured number below comes from that run, and each is marked with the date. Where we could not confirm a feature or a price on the day, we say so in brackets instead of guessing.

Setup and access: who can log in, and from where

Zoho Books runs in a browser, with mobile apps for phone and tablet. You create an organisation, invite users and give each one a role. Your CA joins as an accountant user, and no data file changes hands. A partner at a client site in Udaipur can approve a bill from a phone.

Tally Prime installs on a Windows PC. A multi-user licence lets several PCs in one office work on the same company data. Beyond that office, access needs extra setup: a cloud-hosted Tally from a partner, or the vendor's remote options [confirm current options: as of DATE]. Backups are your job, so decide who copies the data folder, how often and where.

Who wins: Zoho Books for any team that is not always in one room. Tally Prime for a single-office team with a trained accountant and dependable IT.

GST invoices, e-invoicing and returns

Both produce GST-compliant tax invoices and keep the data you need for GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B. A services firm bills mostly on SAC codes at 18%, so the invoice template matters more than stock features. We checked four things on each: SAC on every line, place of supply, the reverse-charge flag and the e-invoice QR code where your turnover requires it [e-invoice turnover threshold: as of DATE].

Zoho Books generates e-invoices and can file returns from inside the product [which plan includes this: as of DATE]. Tally Prime prepares return data and exports it for the portal; some online steps need the vendor's connected services [as of DATE]. For input tax credit, both let you compare purchase data against GSTR-2B. Run that comparison every month, not at return time.

Who wins: a tie on compliance. Before you buy, confirm that your plan or licence covers e-invoicing at your turnover, and decide on the other criteria.

Daily entry: speed for the person doing the books

Tally Prime is built on vouchers and keyboard shortcuts. A trained accountant posts payments and receipts with F5 and F6 without touching the mouse, which is why many Indian accountants will not move. Zoho Books is form driven: clearer for a new joiner, slower for someone with ten years of Tally habit.

On the test file, posting the same [N] vouchers took [N minutes] in Tally Prime and [N minutes] in Zoho Books with our trained accountant. Ask your own accountant to repeat the test. The result depends on the person more than the product.

Who wins: Tally Prime if your accountant already knows it. Zoho Books if you are hiring or training someone from scratch.

Client billing: retainers, payment links, reminders

This is where a services firm lives. Zoho Books has recurring invoices, automatic payment reminders, a client portal and online payment links through supported gateways [which gateways: as of DATE]. A monthly retainer for six clients is set once and goes out on schedule.

Tally Prime treats an invoice as a voucher you enter each time [confirm whether the current release has a recurring-invoice option: as of DATE]. If it does not, a retainer means copying last month's invoice, and reminders go out from your side by email or WhatsApp.

Who wins: Zoho Books, clearly, for any firm sending more than a handful of invoices a month.

Reports, audit trail and your auditor

Tally Prime's ledger and trial balance drill-down is what most Indian auditors grew up on. Your statutory auditor will likely read a Tally file without a briefing, and the edit log shows what changed after posting [confirm: as of DATE]. Zoho Books gives the standard reports (profit and loss, balance sheet, receivables ageing) and an activity log, and the auditor can be invited as a user instead of asking for a file. Both export to Excel.

Who wins: Tally Prime on auditor familiarity. Zoho Books if your auditor is happy to log in. Tell your auditor which product you are choosing before you pay for it.

Support, training and switching later

Tally has the larger partner network, so in most cities a local partner will come to your office [Jaipur partner availability: confirm]. Zoho Books support runs through chat, email and phone [hours: as of DATE], and there are plenty of how-to videos. If your people already know Tally, the cost of retraining them is real and belongs in your decision.

Who wins: Tally Prime for hands-on local support and staff already trained. Zoho Books for self-serve onboarding of new people.

Pricing and total cost

Prices read from the vendors' pages on [DATE].

Zoho Books: a monthly or annual plan per organisation. The users included vary by tier and extra users cost more [plan price as of DATE; users included; extra-user price]. Annual billing is usually cheaper than monthly [confirm: as of DATE].

Tally Prime: a one-time licence, Silver for one user or Gold for several users on a network [licence price as of DATE]. An optional annual support subscription covers updates and connected services [support price as of DATE].

GST at 18% is added to most software prices unless the page says inclusive [confirm: as of DATE]. A GST-registered firm can claim it as input tax credit. Hidden costs: for Zoho, extra users, add-ons and payment-gateway fees; for Tally, the PC or server, backups, partner visit charges and any cloud hosting.

Three-year view for ten people: Zoho is the plan price times 36 plus extra users. Tally is the licence, three years of support, and your IT and hosting. The cheaper one is usually the one with fewer paid users. If only one or two people touch the books, Tally tends to cost less over three years. If six or seven need access, Zoho often does.

Who should choose which

PART 2. REFRESHED ARTICLE

How to file ITR-4 as a freelancer for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27)

Last updated [publish date]: rewritten for FY 2025-26. We rechecked eligibility, the 44ADA and 44AD limits, due dates and late fees. We added an AIS check, a worked example, a mistakes section and an FAQ, and removed the old slab table.

You can file ITR-4 (Sugam) as a freelancer if you are a resident individual with total income up to ₹50 lakh [confirm limit as of DATE]. You must also opt for presumptive taxation under section 44ADA or 44AD. The due date for AY 2026-27 was [date: confirm on the e-filing portal]. If you have missed it, you can still file a belated return until [date: confirm], with a late fee. This guide covers who qualifies, which section applies, what to keep ready and how to file.

Who can use ITR-4, and who cannot

ITR-4 is the short form for presumptive income. You can use it if you are a resident individual, HUF or firm other than an LLP. Your total income must stay within the limit above, and your business or professional income must be taxed on a presumptive basis.

You cannot use ITR-4 if any of the following applies [confirm against the ITR-4 instructions for AY 2026-27]:
- you are a director of a company
- you hold unlisted equity shares
- you own assets outside India or have signing authority on a foreign account
- you want to carry forward a loss
- you want to claim your actual expenses instead of the presumptive profit

In those cases file ITR-3. If you are unsure, check the ITR-4 instructions on the e-filing portal before you start.

Section 44ADA or 44AD: which one is yours

Section 44ADA is for specified professions, such as legal, medical, engineering, architecture, accountancy, technical consultancy and interior decoration, plus others the government has notified. You declare at least 50% of gross receipts as profit. The receipts limit is ₹50 lakh, or ₹75 lakh if cash receipts are no more than 5% of the total [confirm both figures as of DATE].

Section 44AD is for business income. You declare 8% of turnover as profit, or 6% on the part received digitally. The turnover limit is ₹2 crore, or ₹3 crore if cash is no more than 5% [confirm as of DATE].

Many freelancers sit between the two. A consultant or IT professional may fall under 44ADA only if the activity is on the notified list [confirm list as of DATE]. Others file under 44AD. Ask your CA to read the list against your invoices before you choose.

A worked example, for illustration only. A freelance consultant under 44ADA has gross receipts of ₹18,00,000 in FY 2025-26. At 50%, the deemed profit is ₹9,00,000. If you declare less than 50% and your income is above the basic exemption limit, you must keep books and get an audit. That is why most freelancers declare 50% or more.

New regime or old regime

The new tax regime is the default [confirm as of DATE]. If you have business or professional income and want the old regime, you must opt out by filing Form 10-IEA, before the due date of your return. You can switch back to the new regime once. Compare both on your own numbers before you decide. The old regime only wins if your deductions are large. [Confirm slabs, the section 87A rebate and limits as of DATE, and link to the official slab page.]

What counts as gross receipts

Gross receipts are the figure your 50% or 8% is applied to, so get it right. For a professional on the cash method, count every payment you received in the financial year. That includes payments from Indian and foreign clients, platform payouts before the platform's fee, and advances. Count the amount before TDS is cut. GST you collected on behalf of the government is not your income, so keep it out of receipts if your invoices show it separately [confirm treatment with your CA]. Receipts that you cannot match to a bank credit are the first thing a notice will ask about, so keep an invoice for every credit.

Documents to keep ready

- Form 26AS, the Annual Information Statement (AIS) and the Taxpayer Information Summary (TIS), all from the e-filing portal
- Bank statements for every account that received client payments
- Invoices and TDS certificates from clients; the TDS credit should match 26AS and AIS
- GST returns, if you are registered
- Advance tax challans
- Form 10-IEA acknowledgement, if you opted for the old regime
- Aadhaar linked to PAN, for e-verification

Check AIS first. If a client reported a payment that you did not record, resolve it before you file, either by correcting your records or by giving feedback on the AIS entry.

How to file ITR-4 on the portal

1. Log in to the e-filing portal with your PAN.
2. Go to e-File, then Income Tax Returns, then File Income Tax Return.
3. Select the assessment year (AY 2026-27), mode Online, status Individual, and ITR-4.
4. Check the pre-filled personal details and bank accounts. Mark the account where you want any refund.
5. Under business income, enter gross receipts and the presumptive profit for 44ADA or 44AD. Use the same receipts figure as your GST returns, if registered.
6. Enter TDS, advance tax and self-assessment tax paid. Pay any balance tax first and note the challan.
7. Preview the return, submit it, and e-verify within 30 days of filing [confirm window as of DATE]. A return that is not e-verified is treated as not filed.

E-verification works through Aadhaar OTP, net banking, a bank account EVC or a digital signature certificate.

Advance tax for presumptive filers

If you file under 44ADA or 44AD, you can pay your whole advance tax in a single instalment, on or before 15 March of the financial year [confirm as of DATE]. Miss it and interest under sections 234B and 234C applies.

Mistakes freelancers make

- GST turnover and ITR receipts that do not match. The two should reconcile, or you will get a notice. Keep a one-page reconciliation.
- Leaving out receipts from foreign clients. A resident is taxed on income from clients abroad too. Keep FIRC or bank advice for each payment.
- Counting only what reached the bank. Report gross receipts, before TDS and platform fees.
- Skipping AIS and relying on 26AS alone.
- Filing without e-verifying.

A filing calendar that works

- Every month: log each client payment in one sheet, with invoice number, date, TDS and platform fee.
- By 15 March: pay your advance tax in one instalment, if you are a presumptive filer.
- Late April to May: download Form 26AS, AIS and TIS, and chase any client whose TDS is missing.
- June: choose the section and the regime, and file Form 10-IEA if you are opting for the old regime.
- Two weeks before the due date: file, then e-verify the same day [due date: confirm on the portal].

Filing in the last week is the usual mistake. The portal slows down, and any AIS mismatch you find leaves no time to fix.

If you missed the due date

File a belated return under section 139(4) by [date: confirm]. A late fee under section 234F applies, up to ₹5,000, or ₹1,000 if your total income is up to ₹5 lakh [confirm as of DATE]. Interest under section 234A runs at 1% a month on unpaid tax [confirm]. A belated return cannot carry forward most losses, which rarely matters for presumptive filers.

FAQ

Can I claim business expenses under 44ADA? No. The 50% deemed profit is your income after all expenses. If your actual expenses are far higher, ITR-3 with books may suit you better.

Do I need a CA to file ITR-4? No. Many freelancers file on their own. A CA helps when you are choosing between 44ADA and 44AD, or when AIS and your records do not match.

Is ITR-4 right if I also have a salary job? Often yes, if the other income fits the form [confirm the permitted income types for AY 2026-27].

Do I need GST registration as a freelancer? Only if your aggregate turnover crosses the threshold for services, ₹20 lakh in most states and ₹10 lakh in special category states [confirm as of DATE]. If you are registered, your GST returns and your ITR receipts must tell the same story.

What happens after I file? Once you e-verify, the department processes the return and sends an intimation, usually under section 143(1) [confirm]. A refund goes to the pre-validated bank account you marked. Track it under the return's status on the portal. If the intimation shows a demand you do not agree with, you can file a rectification request.

Need help choosing the section or reconciling AIS? Book a call with our team at [booking link].

Socho shaadi ka card. Aap card unhi ko dete ho jinhe aap jaante ho. Review ka bhi yahi hisaab hai.
Chhota sa sawaal. Aapke paas pichhle do mahine ke customers ke numbers kahan hain? Bill book mein, WhatsApp chats mein, ya UPI history mein? Video pause karke ek jagah dhoondh lijiye.

Doosra step: review link.
[SCREEN TEXT: "Step 2: ek tap mein review box"]
Review link ek aisa link hai jo seedha Google ka review box kholta hai. Customer ko aapki dukaan search nahi karni padti.
Address batane aur Maps ka pin bhej dene mein jo fark hai, wahi fark yahan hai. Pin bhejo, aur customer ek tap mein pahunch jaata hai.
Aur ye link aapko banana nahi hai. Google khud deta hai. Abhi screen par dikhata hoon.

Teesra step: message.
[SCREEN TEXT: "Step 3: naam, cheez, ek ask, link"]
Message mein chaar cheezein honi chahiye. Customer ka naam. Usne kya liya. Ek chhota sa request. Aur link.
Aap counter par jaise bolte ho, waise hi likho. Lambi Hindi mat likho. "Namaste ji, ek minute nikaal sakte hain?" kaafi hai.
Dusra chhota sawaal. Aapke message mein customer ka naam aur uska liya hua saamaan hai? Agar nahi, toh wo message copy-paste jaisa lagega, aur copy-paste ka jawab kam aata hai.

Chautha step: ek hi baar yaad dilana.
[SCREEN TEXT: "Step 4: teen din baad, sirf ek baar"]
Kai log message dekhte hain, sochte hain "baad mein karunga", aur bhool jaate hain. Isme unki galti nahi hai. Hum sab aisa karte hain.
Isliye teen din baad ek chhota sa yaad dilana theek hai. "Sunita ji, agar waqt mile toh review ka link yahan hai." Bas itna. Do baar se zyada mat bhejna, warna customer ko pareshani hone lagegi.

4. WORKED EXAMPLE (about 3 minutes)
[SCREEN RECORDING, phone mirrored: Google Maps]
Dikhane ke liye maine ek demo dukaan li hai, "Kesar Namkeen Bhandar". Ye demo profile hai, asli nahi.
Pehle review link nikaalte hain. Maps app kholiye. Upar apni profile photo par tap kijiye. Phir "Your Business Profile" par.
[CUE: tap profile photo, then "Your Business Profile". Confirm labels on screen]
Yahan "Ask for reviews" ya "Share review form" jaisa button milega. Us par tap kijiye. Ab "Copy link" dabaiye.
[CUE: tap Ask for reviews, tap Copy link, show "link copied" toast]
Link copy ho gaya. Ab WhatsApp kholte hain.
[SCREEN RECORDING: WhatsApp, open one chat with a demo customer]
Ek customer chuniye. Maan lo Sunita ji ne pichhle Sunday do kilo mixture liya tha. Main likhta hoon:
[ON SCREEN: type the message slowly]
"Namaste Sunita ji, main Rohan, Kesar Namkeen Bhandar se. Pichhle Sunday aapne do kilo mixture liya tha. Agar ek minute ho toh Google par apna honest review likh dijiye. Isse doosre logon ko hamari dukaan milti hai. Link: [paste]. Dhanyavaad."
[CUE: paste link, show full message]
Ek cheez dhyaan se dekhiye. Maine "accha review" nahi maanga. Maine "honest review" maanga. Ye zaroori hai. Hum sirf achhe reviews nahi khareed rahe. Hum logon ko apni baat likhne ka asaan raasta de rahe hain.
Ek aur baat. Message chhota rakhiye. Phone ki screen par chhe-saat line se lambi cheez log padhte hi nahi. Isliye maine sirf chaar cheezein rakhi hain: naam, saamaan, request, link.
Ab ek shortcut. Agar aap WhatsApp Business use karte ho, toh is message ko Quick Reply mein save kar lo.
[SCREEN RECORDING: WhatsApp Business, Settings, Business tools, Quick replies, new reply with shortcut "/review"]
Shortcut "/review" rakh do. Agle customer ko slash review likho, message khud aa jayega. Bas naam badalna mat bhoolna.
Aur agar aap normal WhatsApp use karte ho, toh message Notes app mein rakh lo aur copy-paste karo. Naam har baar apne haath se badlo.
[SCREEN RECORDING: replace "Sunita ji" with the next name, tap send]
Ho gaya. Ek message, ek minute se kam.
Ab customer ki taraf se dekhiye. Link par tap karte hi Google ka review box khulta hai, star chunne ke liye aur likhne ke liye.
[SCREEN RECORDING: second phone or screen share showing the review box opening from the link]
Review aane mein kuch der lag sakti hai. Customer ke post karne ke baad apni Business Profile mein check kijiye, wahan naya review dikhega.
Aur ek aasan sheet banaiye. Chaar columns: naam, kab bheja, jawab aaya ya nahi, review aaya ya nahi.
[SCREEN RECORDING: simple sheet with those four columns, one demo row filled]
Isse aapko pata rahega ki kise yaad dilana hai aur kise nahi.

5. COMMON MISTAKE (about 40 seconds)
[ON CAMERA]
Ab sabse badi galti. Review ke badle discount ya gift dena.
"Review likho, agli baar 10 percent off." Bahut dukaandaar yahi karte hain. Par Google review ke badle kuch bhi dene ki ijazat nahi deta. Aise reviews hataye ja sakte hain, aur profile par bhi asar pad sakta hai.
Dusri galti usi se judi hai. Apne aap ya apne staff se review likhwana. Wo bhi mat karna.
Apna message check karne ka tareeka: usme "discount", "free" ya "offer" jaisa koi shabd hai? Hai, toh hata do.

6. PRACTICE TASK (about 45 seconds)
[ON CAMERA, then task card on screen]
Ab aapka task. Isme lagbhag pandrah minute lagenge.
Pichhle do mahine ke 15 customers chuniye. Review link copy kijiye. Upar wala message apne shabdon mein likhiye, har customer ka naam aur uska liya hua saamaan daaliye. Phir 15 logon ko WhatsApp par bhej dijiye.
Task tab done hai jab 15 messages gaye hon, aur ek sheet ya copy mein 15 naam likhe hon.
Course group mein ek screenshot daaliye, customers ke numbers dhundhle karke. Saath mein likhiye ki aapne kaunsa shabd badla. Aur ek aur member ka screenshot dekh kar ek suggestion zaroor dijiye.
Agar koi customer pooche "kya likhun?", toh unhe kuch mat batana. Bolo, "Jo bhi aapka experience raha, wahi likh dijiye." Aapko unke shabd chahiye, apne nahi.
Bhejne ka achha waqt shaam hai, jab customer free hota hai. Subah ki bhaag-daud mein message dab jaata hai.
Aaj hi bhejiye. Kal par mat chhodiye.
[SCREEN TEXT: "Task: 15 customers, 15 messages, 1 screenshot in the group"]

7. RECAP AND NEXT LESSON (about 30 seconds)
[ON CAMERA]
Teen baatein yaad rakhiye.
Ek: unse maango jo aapko jaante hain.
Do: Google ka review link bhejo, address nahi.
Teen: naam, cheez, ek request, link. Aur kabhi review ke badle kuch mat do.
Agle lesson mein hum dekhenge ki review aane ke baad kya karna hai. Customer ko jawab kaise dena hai, aur agar ek kharab review aa jaye toh paanch line mein kya likhna hai. Wo lesson aap miss mat karna.
Milte hain Lesson 4 mein.

samples.brief: Weekly free issue of 'Paisa Patterns', the beehiiv newsletter of a fictional Mumbai personal-finance creator (35k Instagram followers, 6k subscribers): one essay on why her own SIP stopped at month 7 and the two changes that restarted it. Indian English with light Hinglish; 500-700 words; subject line and preview text; a reply question; one line on what paid members got this week. No specific fund recommendations.
samples.text:
SUBJECT LINE: Why my SIP stopped at month 7
PREVIEW TEXT: Two small changes restarted it. Neither was willpower.

Last Tuesday I opened my investing app to check something unrelated and landed on the SIP calendar. Seven green ticks in a row. Then a blank. I had not cancelled anything. I had just not noticed that it stopped.

Here is what happened. In month 7 my laptop screen cracked and Diwali shopping landed in the same fortnight. On the 5th, when the SIP was due, my account was short. The debit bounced. Same story next month, because I never topped up. After a couple of missed instalments, my fund house cancelled the mandate. (Rules differ by fund house, so check yours.)

And then came the part nobody warns you about. Restarting felt like admitting I had failed. Opening the app meant looking at the gap. So I did not open it. Five months went by on that.

A friend asked me over lunch, "SIP chal rahi hai na?" I said yes without thinking. In my head it was still running. That is the dangerous bit: a stopped SIP looks exactly like a running one until you check.

The money was not the real problem. The date was wrong, and my plan had no room for a bad month.

Change one: I moved the date. I had set the SIP on the 5th because it felt tidy. But my rent, card bill and electricity all land between the 1st and the 7th. I moved it to the day after my salary arrives, when the account is fullest. It is a boring fix. It is also the one that matters most, because a SIP competes with every other bill for the same balance.

Change two: a floor, not zero. I now have two numbers. The SIP amount I want, and a floor of Rs 500 that I drop to in a tight month. Most apps let you pause or change the amount. Pausing is a decision I make with my eyes open. A bounced debit is an accident I find five months later. I would rather make the decision.

Is it working? Too early to say. It has been two cycles. I will tell you in March whether the calendar is still green, and I will tell you if it is not.

That is all. No new app, no spreadsheet of 14 tabs. A better date and a lower floor.

I am not telling you what to buy. This is my story about a habit, not advice, and I am not a SEBI-registered adviser [confirm status]. No fund names here, on purpose.

ONE-MINUTE CHECK (the same slot every week)
Autopay fails silently. On the 6th of each month, I open my bank statement and look for the SIP debit. If it is there, I close the app. If not, I fix it that day. Takes one minute.

Reply to this email and tell me: what is the last good money habit you dropped, and what was going on that month? I read every reply, and next week I will answer a few here.

If you know someone who says "next month se restart karunga", forward this to them.

Paid members got the monthly-check sheet I use and an audio Q&A on emergency funds this week. If you want those, you can join here: [link].

samples.brief: Spoiler-free review of a fictional new 8-episode Hindi OTT thriller, 'Sonepur Junction', set around a Bihar railway town, for a Delhi culture newsletter. English (Indian); 600-800 words; claims backed by specific (invented, in-world) scenes; a counterweight paragraph; a 'watch it if / skip it if' verdict; discloses the free screener.
samples.text:
SONEPUR JUNCTION
Eight episodes, Hindi, on [platform] from [date]. Created by [creator]. About [runtime] an episode. Rating: 3.5 out of 5.

At 2.10 a.m., early in the first episode, a goods train rolls into the station a minute ahead of schedule, and nobody on the platform mentions it. That minute is the whole method of Sonepur Junction: small wrongnesses, noticed by tired people and left to grow. The result is a patient, atmospheric and sometimes slack eight hours.

The setup is simple enough to give away. In a small railway town in Bihar, a goods wagon arrives with its seal broken. A young railway police inspector, new to the town and its habits, has a week to explain it. The show wants mood first and plot second. So the fair standard is not whether it races, but whether the town feels lived in and whether the dread keeps earning its screen time.

Mostly, it does, and the sound design is why. The station's public-address system is used like a character. Announcements of delayed trains arrive over a tea-seller's radio playing an old ghazal, and the two keep colliding. By episode two, a flat voice announcing a late passenger train has become the most unsettling sound in the series. It is a smart choice, and a cheap one, which is the best kind.

The writing is at its best in rooms, not on the tracks. In episode three, the inspector questions a station employee in his railway-quarters kitchen while his wife cooks. A pressure cooker keeps whistling, and the show lets it drown out the sentence that matters, so we have to read the answer on the inspector's face. Nothing is explained, and nothing needs to be. The dialogue has a Bhojpuri-inflected Hindi that sounds like it belongs to these people, not to a writers' room in Mumbai. Even the small talk, about a cousin's marriage and a delayed ration card, carries information.

The show loses its grip in the middle. Around episode five, a Delhi journalist arrives to cover a political rally and exists mostly to ask the questions the locals would never need asked. Her scenes explain the plot to us, in complete sentences, and the oblique storytelling of episode three disappears. The rally subplot then runs for two episodes and ends without touching the main case. Episode six feels like a show waiting for its finale.

The finale, when it comes, is hurried. Two threads that were given the whole season to breathe are tied off in about the time the first episode needs to introduce one. I will not say which, but you will feel the gear change. The villain's closing speech also says aloud what the sound design had told us quietly for seven episodes. It is the one place the show does not trust its own instincts.

The best case against my view: the slowness is deliberate. This is a town where trains run late and nobody is surprised, and a show that moves at that speed is being faithful, not careless. Viewers who like their thrillers as slow procedure, closer to a long night shift than a chase, may find episodes five and six rich where I found them thin. If you take that view, you will rate it higher than I did, and you would not be wrong.

Watch it if you like atmosphere-first thrillers. Watch it if you want a Bihar that is not reduced to gangsters and slogans, and you are happy to let mood do a plot's work for an hour at a time.

Skip it if you want a tight six-hour story, or if you need every episode to end on a hook.

Start with episodes one and three. If those do not hold you, the rest will not.

Disclosure: I watched all eight episodes on a free screener sent by [platform], with no other consideration.

VARSAAD NI VAATO: monsoon folk tales, a bilingual Gujarati-English comic for children
Help Chomasu Studio in Ahmedabad print the first 2,000 copies of a 200-page comic of eleven monsoon tales, with Gujarati and English on every page. Goal: Rs 12,00,000.

VIDEO SCRIPT (about 90 seconds)
[Shot: studio desk, rain on the window, a stack of pencil pages]
"Last July, a nine-year-old niece asked us for a monsoon story. The Gujarati book on our shelf had no pictures. The picture books had snow.
So we started drawing. [Shot: pages flipping] Eleven folk tales about rain, frogs, clouds and a peacock who borrows an umbrella. Two hundred pages. Gujarati on one line, English right under it, so a child can read in either, and a grandparent can read along.
[Shot: printed 24-page sample in hand] This is a real sample, printed on the paper we want to use. Nine of the eleven tales are drawn. Two are still pencil.
What we do not have is the money to print. A first run of 2,000 copies costs Rs 5 lakh at the printer's quote. The rest of the Rs 12 lakh covers finishing the art, editing, packing and shipping.
[Shot: founders to camera] If we reach the goal, we plan to ship in May 2027, ahead of the monsoon. If we do not, you are not charged.
Please back the book. And send it to one person who reads to a child."

THE STORY
Last July our niece asked for a story about the rain. We looked for a Gujarati book with pictures and found nothing written for children today. Folk tales of this region get told aloud, then they fade. We are two illustrators and an editor, and we decided to draw the tales we remember.

Every page carries two languages on purpose. Many Gujarati families we know speak Gujarati at home and do homework in English. A child who reads one line of each learns that neither is the homework language. A grandparent can read the Gujarati line aloud while the child follows the English.

The tales are our own retellings. In one, a frog's wedding is called off because the groom is two hours late, and he is late because he is the rain. In another, a peacock borrows an umbrella from a cloud and has to give it back wet. They are small, funny and a little strange, which is how we remember them. This is the first print run, and the book exists in nine finished tales today because friends and family paid for the early art. We cannot print without you.

WHERE YOUR MONEY GOES (Rs 12,00,000)
- Printing and binding, 2,000 copies, per the printer's written quote of [DATE]: Rs 5,00,000
- Finishing art and colour for the last two tales: Rs 2,60,000
- Gujarati and English editing and proofreading: Rs 80,000
- Packing and courier within India: Rs 1,20,000
- Platform and payment fees [rate: confirm with the platform]: Rs 96,000
- Reserve for GST and other taxes: Rs 70,000
- Contingency for paper-price changes and damaged copies: Rs 74,000

REWARDS
1. Rs 199, Digital edition. PDF in both languages and your name in the thanks page. Delivered April 2027, worldwide.
2. Rs 799, One book. A paperback copy plus the digital edition. Ships May 2027, India only.
3. Rs 1,499, Signed copy. A copy signed by the illustrators plus four monsoon postcards. Ships May 2027, India only.
4. Rs 2,999, Three books. One to keep, two to gift, plus a poster of the tales. Ships May 2027, India only.
5. Rs 14,999, Library pack. 20 copies to a school or library of your choice in Gujarat, and your name on the dedication page. Ships June 2027.

PROOF AND TEAM
Nine of eleven tales are fully drawn, and the 24-page sample in the video is a real printed proof [photos of the proof and three finished spreads]. Our last book was [past project: title, year, copies delivered]. The printer is [printer name, city] and the Gujarati editor is [name], who has edited [previous work]. Chomasu Studio is responsible for delivery, and we will post a progress update every two weeks.

TIMELINE AND RISKS
- Campaign ends [date]. Funds reach us [per platform terms].
- December 2026 to January 2027: finish art, edit both languages.
- February 2027: final proofs and printer slot confirmed.
- March 2027: printing, about three weeks.
- April 2027: digital edition sent, packing begins.
- May 2027: books ship. We have padded two months before the first rain.
The honest risks: the printer may slip, paper prices may move, and some copies may arrive damaged. Our mitigations are a printer deposit once we are funded, a contingency line in the budget, and replacement of any damaged copy at our cost.

FAQ
What if the goal is missed? This is an all-or-nothing campaign [confirm against the platform's funding model]. If we do not reach Rs 12 lakh by [end date], no one is charged.
Do you ship abroad? Only the digital edition, for now. Courier prices for a print copy are too uncertain to promise.
Are rewards taxed? Prices include GST where it applies [confirm with our CA before launch].
Can I change my pledge? Yes, until the campaign ends.
Will the book be sold elsewhere later? Possibly, if the first run sells through. Backers get the first copies, and the signed editions are only available here.
What if you raise more than Rs 12 lakh? Extra funds go to a second printing and to translating the book into Hindi [confirm plan with the team].

BACK THE BOOK
Back a tier above, and then share this page with one person who reads aloud to a child. A 200-page comic about frogs and clouds reaches its first 2,000 readers one share at a time.
